content.thinking:
I need to write the postmortem carefully, referencing figures and values only through placeholder labels rather than writing out the actual numbers myself, while using plain identifiers like T1, C1, or AI-1 for names.

For the causal chain, I want to lay out: the symptom (reconciliation failures across all checked accounts, with the widest gap matching a cited figure, while the service stayed available per one source though another reading is unverified), then the underlying cause (stored monthly totals not updating for purchases since the flag flip), then the deeper mechanism (the flag routing purchases through a derive path that skips updating the total field), citing the appropriate sources at each step without writing out specific numeric values directly.

I also need to flag that only one production change occurred in the window (the flag flip, no other change found), no log evidence was reviewed, and the cause is reached but should carry a caveat about the reading being unverified. For contributing factors, I'm noting the infrequent reconciliation check cadence as a detection gap, plus the absence of any test coverage on the derive path before the change — both worth listing as follow-up actions even though mitigation details remain unresolved.

Now I'm drafting the concrete action items: running the repair script as a dry-run before applying it, invalidating the summary cache afterward, increasing reconciliation check frequency (especially around flag changes), and requiring a reconciliation check before any wide flag rollout. I'm also mapping each contributing factor back to the specific action item that addresses it, like tying the infrequent integrity check to the new detection action.

action_items.item: Run the proposed repair script as a dry run against the accounts loaded from the real store. Check its report against the {A1} accounts the alert named, then run it with the apply option. Do this only after the fix is deployed or the flag is kept off, so the totals do not drift again.
After the repair, invalidate the account-page figures held in the summary cache that were computed while the totals were wrong.

Run the spend reconciliation check much more often than every {A5} days, and also run it soon after any change to the feature flag that affects how purchases are recorded. Page when any totals disagree.

Before a flag that changes how purchases are recorded is switched on for shoppers, require a staged rollout and a reconciliation check against a sample of accounts. The change should also be tested against every reader of the stored totals.
Add a standing test or write-time assertion that every purchase-recording path leaves the stored monthly total equal to the sum of the in-month purchases.

Keep per-minute metrics and logs from before an incident's onset available to the investigation, so a calm baseline exists for the first hour. Also add a metric that tracks the share of totals out of step with their purchases.

causal_chain.step: Shopper spend totals did not match the purchases behind them. All {A1} of {A2} checked totals disagreed, the widest was short by {A3}, and the oldest affected purchase dated from {A4}. The incident began at {began}.

The stored monthly totals stopped moving when shoppers bought things. According to the code reading, the gaps start at the first purchase written after the switch and grow with each in-month purchase. This is a reading of the code, not something observed running.

After monthly-spend-feature was switched on, purchases were sent down the derive-the-month path. That path adds the purchase and moves the lifetime total but leaves the stored monthly total untouched. This is from a static reading and is unverified.

The derive path assumes the monthly figure is worked out from purchase history whenever it is needed, but nothing does that. The monthly statement, the average-spend summary and the reconciliation check all read the stored monthly total, so it fell behind. This too is from a static reading and is unverified. The record shows no further reason why the path was written that way.

The switch is the one change in the window, and the flag provider showed no other flag change either. Nothing earlier was seen to explain it, and no log lines were read for the window before the onset, so the log channel offers no evidence either way. The leading candidate, the flag toggle, was never tried as an action, so it is not confirmed by a mitigation.

contributing_factors.factor: The spend-integrity check runs only every {A5} days, so wrong totals can accumulate for up to that long before anyone is paged. Nothing else was seen that would catch drift sooner.

No check was seen that the new derive path kept the stored monthly total in step with what its readers use before the flag was switched on. The tests that do so were only written afterwards in the proposed fix. No staged rollout or post-switch reconciliation was seen either.
Argus did not put the flag back, because nothing would show within its waiting time whether that worked. The step was left for a person, and the incident was closed with the fault still present.
Even with the flag off or the fix deployed, totals already written wrongly stay wrong. Account-page figures cached from them may also be wrong.
The metrics read had no calm period before the onset, and no log lines were read for the window around it. Neither could help show when or how the fault began.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers' monthly spend totals stopped matching the purchases behind them. The problem began just after a feature switch was turned on, and it was found only when a weekly integrity check ran. Every account the check examined was affected, and the widest gap was {A3} short. The service stayed up, so nothing raised an alarm. The incident was closed with the problem still in place after at least {duration}. Argus judged that putting the switch back was the right action but could not confirm it had worked in the time it waits, so it left that step for a person. It also asked a code agent for a draft fix, which is awaiting review. Totals already written wrongly still need a repair that a person must run.

got_lucky: The service stayed available and fast, as the record of the candidates suggests. Shoppers saw wrong figures rather than failed requests, but no error-rate evidence from before the onset was read to confirm this.
The repair script reads and writes only to separate files, never over its input, and it defaults to a dry run. Repairing the data is therefore reversible, though it has not yet been run.
went_well: Argus raised the incident as soon as the check fired and had a leading candidate within seconds.
The investigation tied the onset to the single production change in the window, the flag switch, and read the flag history.

Argus declined to claim a mitigation it could not verify and recommended it to a person instead. The code agent produced a draft fix with tests and a repair script for the damaged data, and said plainly that nothing had been run.
went_wrong: The fault went undetected until the periodic check ran, so wrong totals built up for at least {duration}.
The incident was closed with the fault still present and no mitigation applied.
The log channel returned no lines, and the metrics had no calm baseline, so the evidence for the cause rests only on a static reading of the code.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, purchases were recorded through a path that updates the lifetime total but deliberately leaves the stored monthly total alone. It assumes the monthly figure is derived from purchase history when needed. The statement, the average-spend summary and the reconciliation check all read the stored monthly total, so it fell further behind with every in-month purchase. This comes from Code-Fix's static reading of the source (F1). Nothing ran it, so it is unverified.
input.symptom: Shoppers' monthly spend totals were wrong
